Return the full citation, PMID/DOI, sample size, pre/post timing, satisfaction instrument/items, statistical comparisons, and the authors’ conclusion about whether renovation biased satisfaction ratings.'}

## PubMed result

The title appears in PubMed without the leading “Is”:

**Tièche R, da Costa BR, Streit S.** Patient satisfaction is biased by renovations to the interior of a primary care office: a pretest-posttest assessment. **BMC Health Serv Res.** 2016;16:373. Published August 11, 2016.  
**PMID:** 27515540  
**DOI:** [10.1186/s12913-016-1647-4](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-016-1647-4)  
**PMCID:** PMC4982145

A closely related follow-up was also identified: **“Interior renovation of a general practitioner office leads to a perceptual bias on patient experience for over one year”** (PLOS ONE, 2018; PMID 29462196).

## Study details

- **Design/location:** Pretest–posttest observational study in a single primary-care practice in Grenchen, Switzerland.
- **Sample:** Two analyzed consecutive patient samples of **153 before renovation and 153 after renovation** (**306 total**). The overall response rate was approximately **85%**. The full-text results note that **16 post-renovation respondents were excluded** because they had attended the practice for less than two months and therefore had not seen the office before renovation.
- **Timing:** Satisfaction was measured before the interior renovation and again after renovation. For the post-renovation analysis, patients needed at least **two months’ exposure/attendance** to have been able to compare the renovated and former environments. The abstract does not specify calendar dates for the two survey waves.
- **Satisfaction instrument:** A study questionnaire covering **four domains**:
  1. Appearance/interior of the office  
  2. Qualities of the medical assistants  
  3. Qualities/skills of the general practitioners  
  4. Overall/general patient satisfaction  

  It used **12 quality indicators**, each rated on a **six-point Likert scale** from **1 = very poor** to **6 = very good**.

## Statistical comparisons

- Pre- versus post-renovation satisfaction was compared using domain-level scores.
- Satisfaction was **higher after renovation in all four domains**, with reported significance ranging from **p < 0.01 to p < 0.001**.
- A multivariable analysis incorporating potential confounders produced essentially the same result, with effects remaining significant at **p < 0.01**.
- The retrieved PubMed/full-text extract does not identify the precise named univariate test used for each comparison; therefore, it is safest to report the published significance levels and adjusted-model result rather than assign a specific test.

## Authors’ conclusion

The authors concluded that renovating the office interior was associated with improved patient satisfaction, including ratings of domains that were not themselves changed by the renovation. They interpreted this as evidence that the physical environment can **bias patients’ assessments of medical-care quality**—including their assessments of physician skills—and recommended accounting for such contextual effects when designing patient quality-assessment instruments.

**Bottom line:** Yes. The study’s conclusion was that interior renovation **did bias upward post-renovation satisfaction ratings**, not merely ratings of the office appearance but also ratings of medical care and provider-related domains.

The targeted search identified the exact article and provides the key outcome: post-renovation ratings rose across all four satisfaction domains, including unchanged care-related domains. I’ll now store the paper and findings, then review the evidence record before concluding.

The evidence supports **yes**.

The relevant study was:

- **Tièche R, da Costa BR, Streit S.** *Patient satisfaction is biased by renovations to the interior of a primary care office: a pretest-posttest assessment.* **BMC Health Services Research.** 2016;16:373. PMID: **27515540**.

### Findings

- Single primary-care practice in Switzerland.
- Patient surveys were conducted before and after renovation, with **153 patients in each period**.
- The questionnaire assessed:
  - Office appearance
  - Medical assistants
  - General practitioners
  - Overall satisfaction
- Ratings increased significantly after renovation across **all four domains**—including perceptions of physicians and staff, whose clinical work was not directly altered.
- Reported significance levels ranged from **p < 0.01 to p < 0.001**, and adjusted analyses remained significant.

### Interpretation

The pattern suggests a **contextual or perceptual bias**: an improved physical environment may have positively influenced patients’ evaluations of care quality beyond their assessment of the renovated space itself.

The study was observational and conducted in one practice, so it cannot establish universal causality. Nevertheless, its pretest–posttest findings directly support the conclusion that interior renovations can bias patient-satisfaction ratings upward.

FINAL DECISION: YES
